newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Data may steal FOMC's thunder.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Data may steal FOMC's thunder.

text.p: For a change, economic data releases appeared to be overshadowing a policy-making meeting of the U.S. central bank.
The Federal Reserve's Federal Open Market Committee meets next Tuesday and Wednesday, but economists widely dismissed the chances of any further tightening of monetary policy.

Instead, the focus for the week would be on the National Association of Purchasing Management's June survey on Tuesday and the June nonfarm payrolls report on Thursday as analysts tried to detect signals of accelerated economic growth.

When the Fed's policy-making arm met on March 25, it voted to hike the federal funds rate -- the interest rate banks charge each other for overnight loans -- by 25 basis points. However, the FOMC took no action at its May meeting and economists would look to next week's data for signs the Fed may vote to tighten again at its August meeting.

In addition to NAPM and payrolls, the market also would digest personal income and consumption, new home sales and the Chicago purchasers' report on Monday; construction spending and leading economic indicators on Tuesday; and factory orders on Wednesday. Car sales were set throughout the week.
Second quarter economic growth cooled considerably from the first quarter, but many economists expected a resurgence even as the current recovery was in its sixth year.
Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan has said he would look to signs of strong economic growth rather than overt inflationary signals as a cue to further monetary tightening.
"At the beginning of the week we probably will see some window dressing for quarter end," said Michael Strauss, chief economist at Sanwa Securities (USA) Co.
He saw the positive tone the market has seen remaining regardless of what Monday's numbers showed.

Strauss said there continued to be some nervousness ahead of Thursday's employment report -- to be released early due to the July 4 Independence Day holiday in the United States on Friday. The PSA, the Bond Market Trade Association, also recommended an early close of 1500 EDT/1900 GMT on Thursday.
"Some see retracement as we move into early July," Strauss said. He expected nonfarm payrolls to rise by 235,000 in June, and the May figure to be revised upward.
John Mueller, senior vice president and chief economist at Lehrman Bell Mueller Cannon Inc, said there was a strong possibility the bond market would turn weaker next week.

Mueller said a string of weaker economic reports in the second quarter gave credence to many economists' views that growth had slowed to a 2.0 percent range in the second quarter. However, it was likely to pick up to 3.0 percent to 3.5 percent in the third quarter, he said.
A pickup in retail sales could be seen and "the bond market has gone a little bit too far and could be caught (in a correction)," Mueller said.
There was a lot more room for surprises on the downside than on the upside, Mueller said.
Late Friday, the Treasury's 30-year bond was trading at 98-14/32, up 14/32, to yield 6.75 percent.

At the short end of the maturity spectrum the three-month bill rate was up two basis points at 5.01 percent. Six-month bills were unchanged at 5.03 percent, and year-bills were down 1/32 at 5.32 percent.
Five-year notes were up 3/32 at 99-20/32, yielding 6.34 percent. Ten-year notes were up 8/32 at 101-9/32, yielding 6.45 percent.
